To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the incidence of AKI requiring dialysis among hospitalized adults with an associated diagnosis HIV infection has increased from 2002–2010 and that this rise is completely explained by ageing of this population and an increase in chronic non-AIDS co-morbidities and procedures.

the incidence of severe AKI requiring dialysis continues to increase among hospitalized adults with an associated diagnosis HIV infection, and this increase is largely explained by ageing, increased comorbidities (including chronic non-AIDS diseases) and increased utilization of procedures.

the incidence of AKI requiring dialysis among hospitalized adults with an associated HIV infection increased from 0 to 1.3% between 2002 and 2010 and that the odds of in-hospitals mortality associated with this complication increased over the same time frame, from 1 to 3.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a growing problem in HIV-infected adults that requires further investigation and intervention.
a growing population of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and HIV infection.
a very serious condition, acute kidney injury (‘AKI’), that can lead to death or the need for long-term kidney dialysis.

the increasing prevalence of dialysis-requireing AKI in HIV-infected adults is largely explained by ageing and the increasing prevalence of chronic comorbidities.
the incidence of acute renal failure requiring dialysis is increasing and that this is associated with an increase in mortality in hospitalized patients with HIV.
the incidence of AKI requiring dialysis among hospitalized adults with AIDS has increased, and this increase is largely explained by the aging of the HIV population.

the burden of dialysis AKI in the hospitalised HIV population continues to increase, with a concomitant increase in the associated odds of death.
